tagline: A blue line on a planning map became a contested suburban expressway
intro: The Blue Route carries I-476 through the Philadelphia suburbs between Plymouth Meeting and I-95 near Chester, crossing the Schuylkill River and following part of the Crum Creek valley. Wooded stretches lie between US 1 and Broomall. PennDOT records its legislative byway designation in 1993; Visit Pennsylvania highlights access to places including Ridley Creek State Park and Tyler Arboretum.

The project had been planned as early as 1929; in 1954 the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission proposed it as the Chester Extension, before it became an Interstate project. The name began with a 1958 planning map: a blue alignment through the Crum Creek valley was chosen over red, yellow and green alternatives. Construction began in 1967, but environmental lawsuits involving PennDOT and communities along the route extended the work over decades. A 1985 agreement reshaped the design, including a four-lane section south of PA 3 and restrictions on advertising billboards.

Heading south from Plymouth Meeting, cross the Schuylkill on the Pearl Harbor Memorial Bridge to West Conshohocken. At Radnor’s US 30 interchange, stone artworks commemorate the Welsh Tract. Continue through Broomall and past US 1 to the creek corridor through Swarthmore and Wallingford, then MacDade Boulevard and the I-95 junction near Chester.

moments.title: Pearl Harbor Memorial Bridge
moments.text: The Pearl Harbor Memorial Bridge carries the Blue Route across a river corridor shared by freight trains, commuter rail and a trail. Below are the Schuylkill, Norfolk Southern’s Harrisburg Line, SEPTA’s Manayunk/Norristown Line and the Schuylkill River Trail. The trail itself occupies the former track bed of the Pennsylvania Railroad’s Schuylkill Valley Division, which opened in 1884 and lost rail service in the 1970s. South of the crossing, I-476 meets I-76 at West Conshohocken. SEPTA’s line follows tracks built along the river in 1835 for the Philadelphia, Germantown, and Norristown Railroad.

moments.title: The Radnor griffin
moments.text: A griffin made from crushed stone spreads across a hillside at the US 30 interchange. A large stone cairn stands on the hilltop. These monuments commemorate Radnor’s history as part of the Welsh Tract. They belong to the Radnor Gateway Enhancement Strategy, which brought large sculptural works by artist William P. Reimann to the interchange.
moments.notice: The interchange’s stonework includes a hilltop cairn and a griffin formed from crushed stone.

moments.title: Crum Creek
moments.text: Crum Creek gave the selected blue line on the planning map its course through the suburbs. South of US 1, the freeway follows the creek through Wallingford and Swarthmore. The four-lane design south of PA 3 was one of the environmental compromises in the 1985 agreement. Rail crossings punctuate this stretch: I-476 runs beneath SEPTA’s Media/Wawa Line and over its light rail Media–Sharon Hill Line. At MacDade Boulevard, the creek-parallel parkway section reaches Woodlyn, before the road’s southern end at I-95 near Chester. The creek also forms Springfield Township’s western boundary before flowing south to the Delaware River.
